Stop logging Chronicle connection string credentials (#3611)

* Add credential redaction to the Chronicle connection string

A connection string carries the OAuth client secret, the API key and the
certificate password. Nothing could render it without them, so every
diagnostic use of one was a credential in clear text.

BuildRedacted() masks the modelled credentials, and falls back to the option
name for the ones the builder does not model - a connection string carries
arbitrary options, and over-redacting a value costs a little diagnostic
detail where under-redacting one puts it in the log forever.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Stop logging the client secret when connecting to Chronicle

Both connection log messages passed the ChronicleConnectionString itself, so
the formatter rendered it through ToString() - client secret, API key and
certificate password included - at Information level, on every connect and
every watchdog reconnect. Pass the redacted rendering instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Document redacting a connection string for logs

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Drop the redundant Class flag from the generated client type attributes

TypeAttributes.Class is 0x0, so a Roslynator brought in by the latest
package update flags 'Public | Class' as a flag already contained in
another (RCS1258) and fails the client snippet verification build.

* Redact by masking the values, not by rendering conditionally

BuildRedacted() threaded a redactSecrets flag through the whole of Build(),
so which credentials reached the result depended on a runtime branch - and a
helper that can return either the mask or the real value is one CodeQL flags
as clear-text logging at every call site, correctly in the sense that nothing
about the shape of the code rules the secret out.

Build a copy that holds no credential at all and render that instead. The
guarantee is now structural rather than conditional, and Build() goes back to
being one unconditional renderer.

The mask is REDACTED rather than ***, because a query parameter value goes
through Uri.EscapeDataString and *** came out as %2A%2A%2A there while the
userinfo kept ***. One mask that survives escaping keeps every redacted value
looking the same.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Prevent projection registration storms (#3666)

* Skip registration work for projection definitions that have not changed

Every client replica re-registers its full definition set on startup and
on every reconnect. The projections manager grain processed the full set
every time - engine registration on every silo, SetDefinition on every
projection grain and an observer subscription per definition and
namespace - even when nothing had changed. Because the grain is
non-reentrant, a registration that outlived its caller's timeout kept
its retries queueing the same workload behind it, and the queue never
drained (the production registration storm).

Compare each incoming definition against the registered state with the
same comparer the projection grain uses for replay decisions, and only
process the ones that are new or different. An identical re-registration
returns immediately, which also collapses a queue of identical requests:
the first does the work, the rest compare equal and answer near-free.
The state is only merged after the engine and the projection grains have
accepted the definitions, so an interrupted registration is retried in
full instead of being skipped as unchanged. Event type schemas are now
fetched once per registration pass instead of once per definition and
namespace.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add specs for the projections manager grain registration paths

Cover the unchanged fast path, the changed and new definition paths,
a mixed batch where only some definitions changed, and the collapsing
of an identical registration arriving a second time.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Run RegisterAll as a single flight with backoff between failed runs

A registration request that times out client-side is usually still
queued kernel-side, and every path that re-triggered registration - a
reconnect, or any operation re-running connect after a failed run -
immediately sent the kernel another copy of the same registration to
queue behind the first. Stacked across replicas this is the feedback
loop behind the production registration storm.

RegisterAll now runs as a single flight per event store: callers that
arrive while a run is in flight await that same run instead of starting
another, and a run that follows a failure waits an exponentially
growing, jittered delay (1s doubling, capped at one minute) before
hitting the wire, so a kernel that is slow to accept a registration
sees retry pressure back off instead of pile up. A successful run
resets the backoff.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add specs for registration single flight and backoff

Cover sharing an in-flight run, invoking again after completion,
backing off after a failed run and resetting on success, the backoff
delay growth, cap and jitter bounds, and that a second RegisterAll
arriving while one is in flight sends the kernel a single registration.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Pin the read model shape guards that no spec could falsify (#3668)

* Pin the unset-property guards a mutation could not reach

The guards that stop an unset read model property being written as a
schema-forbidden default shipped in 16.16.0, but most of them were not
falsifiable. The nullable-enum spec picked a subject both guards suppress,
so deleting the nullability leg left it green and only a nullable boolean
in a differently-named file noticed. The member-list check had no subject
at all: no fixture anywhere declared an enum whose zero is a real member,
so inverting that check left the entire suite green while silently
dropping a value the model legitimately projected.

Both now have subjects that isolate them. A nullable enum declaring a zero
member can only be suppressed by nullability, and a non-nullable one
declaring a zero member must still be written - that second case is the
contract's stated non-goal and nothing was holding it.

The schemas these guards read were only ever hand written in specs, so
nothing checked that the generator emits the shape they expect. A future
change to how nullability is rendered would have un-fixed this silently,
with every spec passing. The generator specs pin that wire, and the replay
recommendation specs pin the operator-visible consequence, which moved for
a non-nullable enum and was covered only for strings.

No production behavior changes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Pin the children-path exclusion that nothing could falsify

A root event must not write an empty children collection, because a
parallel replay would set a populated array back to empty and race a
sibling partition's already-added child away. The exclusion that prevents
this has been in the pipeline for a while, and the in-process harness was
taught to apply it too so specs stop disagreeing with the live sink.

Nothing could tell whether either still worked. The walk that collects the
children paths had no spec at all, the only spec calling the changeset
helper omitted the argument that reaches the exclusion branch, and the
pipeline-step spec asserted merely that some property was added. Removing
the exclusion outright left the whole suite green while restoring the
defect it exists to prevent.

Each of those now has a spec that dies to it alone, including the nested
case, which the recursion needs to be pinned separately from the root
filter. The harness assertions are extended to the per-key view, which was
reading through different serializer options than the one that was pinned.

No production behavior changes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Assert the precondition that arms the unset-optional integration spec

The spec reaches the code it fences only because its read model carries a
PII value, which is what sends the whole state through the registered
schema on the way into the sink. Nothing asserted that. Disabling
compliance detection left every assertion in the file green: the released
value reads back as plaintext either way, and the unset property is absent
because the round trip never happened at all rather than because the guard
under test held.

The stored document was already being read for the other at-rest
assertions, so pinning it costs one comparison. Both independent reviewers
found this hole separately, which is a fair signal it is easy to miss.

Diagnose inert stream metadata and a split duplicate context mapping (#3670)

* Report a duplicate context mapping split across parameter and property

The diagnostic already caught two [SetFromContext] for one event type on a
member, but only when both attributes sat on the same symbol. On a
positional record they need not: one can target the primary constructor
parameter and the other the generated property, and those are two symbols.
Grouping them apart meant the analyzer stayed silent while both mappings
still reached the builder under the same key, where the property pass runs
second and quietly wins - the exact discard the diagnostic exists to
report, reachable through a spelling it could not see.

A positional record's generated property is now paired off against its
parameter and the parameter carries the union of both symbols' attributes,
so the pair is judged as the single member a reader sees. Declared
properties with no matching parameter keep their own path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Diagnose stream metadata declared on an event type, which does nothing

Both attributes documented themselves as applying to an event type, a
command or an observer. Only the last two are read: the sole consumers
take the metadata off a reactor, a reducer or a command type, and an
append resolves stream metadata from its own parameters. Declaring either
on an event type therefore compiles, reads as deliberate, and has no
effect anywhere.

The documentation is corrected and a diagnostic now reports the
placement, so the mistake is caught where it is written rather than
discovered by an observer that never sees the events it was meant to
narrow.

Honoring the placement instead was deliberately not done. Both values are
persisted in every appended event's context and key concurrency scopes and
observer filtering, so letting an event type contribute them would
retroactively change stream identity for every event type already
declared, against data already written.

Scoped to the two attributes that made the claim. FilterEventsByTag is
equally inert on an event type but never documented that placement, so
reporting it would be a new break with nothing behind it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Stop the diagnostic flagging types that do read stream metadata

Narrowing the documentation to a command or an observer was itself wrong:
an aggregate root reads the stream type off its own attribute, and falls
back to its type name when the attribute is absent. Telling an author it
belongs elsewhere invites them to delete it, and deleting it does not
error - every event that aggregate appends silently lands under a
different stream type. That is the damage this diagnostic exists to
prevent, created by the correction. Only the stream type is affected;
nothing reads the source type off an aggregate root, and its wording is
left alone.

The diagnostic itself flagged the same shape. It keyed only on the event
type attribute, so a type that is both a command and an event type, or a
reactor carrying an event type, was told to move an attribute that is
live on it - a warning this repository treats as an error, on a false
claim. It now skips a type that is read by any of those roles.

The specs that were supposed to cover the roles carried them as
decoration: the analyzer never looked at either, so both passed only
because the type was not an event type. They now carry both, which left
the event-type guard itself unpinned, so a spec whose subject reaches it
was added. Every guard now has an input that arrives at it.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

Run the production image in Aspire production mode, and let it be given certificates (#3679)

* Use the production image when Aspire is configured for production

The production branch selected the development-slim tag, contradicting
the method's own documentation. Only the development images are compiled
with the DEVELOPMENT symbol, so an AppHost that configured Chronicle for
production was running a development-compiled kernel.

AddCratisChronicle had no specs at all -- the existing Aspire specs cover
only the MongoDB builder -- so nothing could have caught this and nothing
goes red when it is corrected. The specs added here enumerate the two
modes and the naming, and the production tag is pinned from both sides.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Let an Aspire application supply Chronicle's certificates

Selecting the production image is only half an answer: that image refuses
to start without a TLS certificate, and the OAuth authority refuses
without an encryption certificate. Neither could be configured through
the Aspire builder at all, so the corrected production path could not
boot -- a worse outcome than the wrong image it replaced.

Both certificates are separate methods rather than one. They configure
unrelated subsystems, fail independently, and either can legitimately be
present without the other; folding them together would take four
positional strings and make "TLS only" inexpressible.

Each mounts the file read-only into the container and points the
configuration at the path inside it. Setting a host path would name a
file the container cannot see, and making the consumer remember a
matching bind mount is boilerplate the framework can own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Pin the published image names and configuration keys

Every assertion compared a tag to the constant it came from, so nothing
asserted what the constants say. Repointing the production tag at the
development image, or at a tag that does not exist, left the whole suite
green while every AppHost pulled the wrong thing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Read a TLS certificate as PKCS#12 whether or not it carries a password

Without a password the loader took a path that reads DER and PEM only,
so a password-less .pfx did not merely lose its private key -- the server
died with "ASN1 corrupted data" and never started. The password-protected
path was fine, which is why this survived: the common case worked.

It is a regression from the X509CertificateLoader migration. The branch
this replaced read PKCS#12 correctly on the previous target framework.

TLS needs the private key that only PKCS#12 carries, so reading anything
else could never have produced a usable certificate. There is nothing for
the password to select between.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

* Fail fast on a missing certificate, and let a later call win

Docker creates a directory when a bind mount's source does not exist, so
a mistyped certificate path produced a container whose kernel reported
that no certificate was configured -- the opposite of the truth -- while
the process died and the container still read as running. The path is now
resolved against the app host directory and checked before it is mounted.

Configuring either certificate twice appended a second mount on the same
target, which Docker refuses outright. Every other method on this builder
is last-call-wins, so a base helper with an override produced a container
that could not start. The later call now replaces the earlier one, down to
clearing a password the overriding call does not supply.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UWugkmN6NmoemKeTvSKNDg

Add an opt-in health-only dedicated listener (#3695)

* Add an opt-in health-only dedicated listener

The dedicated health port was a second Kestrel endpoint on the same
WebApplication, and every HTTP/1.1 route was mapped app-wide with no port
predicate - so the Workbench, REST API and OAuth endpoints were reachable
on it too. The Kernel Server is a sealed top-level Program, so a consumer
could not add the filter themselves and network policy was the only
mitigation.

health.exclusive short-circuits any path other than the health endpoint
on that port. It keys on the connection's local port rather than a header,
so nothing a client sends can reach the restricted surface. Default off,
so existing deployments are unchanged.

The decision is extracted into HealthOnlyPortPolicy so it can be specced -
Program.cs top-level statements are otherwise unreachable from a spec.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Match routing exactly when deciding what the health port serves

The path check trimmed whitespace from the request path, which routing
does not. "/health%20" decodes to "/health ", so the check trimmed it to
"/health" and admitted it, while routing saw a different path, missed
MapHealthChecks and fell through to the fallback - serving the Workbench
entry document with 200 on a port advertised as health-only.

The request path now gets only the normalization routing itself performs:
trailing slash ignored, case-insensitive, nothing else. The configured
endpoint is operator-supplied rather than attacker-supplied and is still
trimmed. An endpoint that is missing or only whitespace now matches
nothing and the port rejects everything, instead of resolving to "/" and
serving the fallback.

Found by security review before merge.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Diagnose passive re-keying and inert clear declarations (#3702)

* Diagnose passive re-keying and inert clear declarations

CHR0046 covers the hazard documented in v16.24.0 but not yet detected: a
passive read model whose projection redirects the root document key.
Passive reads have no sink, so the kernel answers by replaying with the
cursor constrained to the requested key - it walks one event source. A
top-level re-key is routing metadata, not a lookup index, so events
appended on another stream are never seen and the read returns a default
initialized model. It registers fine and ReadModelScenario still passes,
which is why nothing catches it today.

CHR0047 covers two declarations that compile and then do nothing. A null
SetValue is parsed and dropped - every consumer guards on non-null, and
the member is registered as mapped before the guard, which also suppresses
the no-mapping-source diagnostic. And a property-level ClearWith binds to
nothing, because the only consumer reads class-level attributes on the
nested type; the attribute permits three targets and one is read.

Both are warnings on the precedent already written into KeyRedirectionPii
and CHR0044: a first-release conservative rule warns rather than breaking
a build transitively.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Catch the null-forgiving form the compiler actually allows

A bare null in [SetValue] raises CS8625 - the attribute parameter is
non-nullable - so anyone who writes this declaration at all writes null!
to get past the compiler. The documentation snippet did not compile for
that reason, which is what surfaced it.

GetConstantValue already folds through the suppression, so the rule
reported it correctly; that behavior is now pinned by a spec rather than
assumed, since a rule that caught only the version nobody can ship would
be worth nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Say where a value's subject comes from rather than what to do with it (#3706)

[ReleaseUnder] named the action rather than the information: it told the
release pass what to do, when what the declaration actually carries is
where to find the subject. [SubjectFrom] says that, and reads alongside
[Subject] rather than beside it.

[ReleaseUnder] shipped in v16.20.0 and is public API, so it stays as a
derived alias with its constructor obsoleted rather than being renamed.
Deriving rather than matching both names by hand means the compatibility
path is the new path, so the two cannot drift apart. The deprecation sits
on the constructor because applying the attribute is the only way to
consume it - and because marking the type obsolete makes the type
discovery generator emit warnings in generated code no one can suppress.

The two refusal types keep their names. Renaming them would break catch
clauses for no benefit, since the ruling was about the declaration; their
messages name the new attribute.
